opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to the fact that language is a really compressed, discrete, symbolic interface, and it evolved largely for communicating between people who already share a huge amount of grounded experience of the world. So when I say "a cup falling off a table," I'm relying on you to fill in all the physics: how it tumbles, how it might shatter, the sound it makes, where the pieces go. The words themselves carry very little of that information. They're pointers into a shared model of the world that we each built mostly through perception and interaction, not through reading.

So if you try to go the other way, and actually describe a perceptual concept fully in language, it gets cumbersome very quickly. Think about trying to describe the exact texture of a surface, or the precise way someone's face changes as they're about to smile, or the trajectory of a ball bouncing off an irregular wall. You end up writing paragraphs and you still haven't really pinned it down. A lot of perceptual knowledge is continuous, high-dimensional, and kind of tacit. It's intuitive physics, spatial relationships, fine-grained motion, and language just isn't a very efficient basis for representing that.

That's a big part of the motivation behind the work we've been doing on joint-embedding predictive architectures, like I-JEPA and V-JEPA. Instead of grounding everything through text, or trying to reconstruct every pixel, which spends a lot of capacity on unpredictable low-level detail, the idea is to learn by predicting in an abstract representation space directly from sensory input like images and video. The model can then develop its own internal representation of these perceptual concepts, things like object permanence or how motion unfolds, without having to route them through words. Language is incredibly powerful for abstract reasoning and communication, and I don't think it goes away. But if we want systems that really understand the physical world, I think a lot of that understanding has to be learned from perception itself, the way babies and animals learn it, long before any words are involved.

r001.rationale: The response mentions images and video as sensory inputs, but does not say that a few visual examples communicate a perceptual concept more readily than verbal description.

r002.rationale: It gives changing facial expressions and a ball’s bouncing trajectory as examples of perceptual motion, then says fine-grained motion is inefficient to represent in language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd put it is that language is this incredibly compressed, lossy summary of the world. It evolved as a tool for communicating between people who already share a huge amount of perceptual grounding. So when I say "the cup is on the table," I'm leaning on the fact that you already know what a cup looks like, what "on" means physically, how gravity works, what happens if I nudge it toward the edge. None of that is actually in the sentence. The sentence is just a pointer into a world model that we both already have.

The problem is when you try to build a system that learns about the physical world primarily through language, you're asking it to reconstruct all of that grounding from the pointers alone. And there's a lot of stuff that's just really awkward to put into words. Think about describing exactly how a piece of cloth folds when it falls, or the precise way a ball bounces off a curved surface, or the subtle difference between how a cat moves versus how a dog moves. You can write paragraphs about it and still not capture what a two-year-old understands just from watching. The information is continuous, it's high-dimensional, it's spatial and temporal, and language is discrete and sequential and relatively low-bandwidth.

So in some sense it's not that language is bad. It's a great interface for abstract reasoning and for communication. But it's a pretty inefficient channel for actually acquiring perceptual and physical concepts in the first place. Humans and animals don't learn those things through language. We learn them by observing and interacting, and then language gets layered on top as a way to label and manipulate concepts we already have. That's a big part of the motivation for the work we've been doing on learning world models directly from video and sensory data, in a representation space rather than in pixels or in tokens. You want the system to form those perceptual abstractions on its own, from observation, and then language becomes something you can attach to that, rather than the thing you're forced to learn everything through.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts verbal descriptions with learning by watching, but does not state that a few visual examples communicate a concept more readily than words.

r002.rationale: It says perceptual information is temporal and uses unfolding or bouncing interactions as examples of details that are awkward to capture in language.

astra-6.text:
I think language is a very powerful abstraction, but it doesn’t necessarily capture all the detail in our perceptual experience. Imagine trying to describe a particular shade of blue, or the exact way an object is moving. You might need a lot of words, and even then, the person listening might have a different picture in mind. If you could just show them, it would be immediately clear.

So when we think about learning representations of the world, language is one useful source of information, but it shouldn’t have to be the interface for everything. There are properties of the visual world that we can learn directly from observations without first having to put them into words.

r001.rationale: It contrasts describing a perceptual detail with showing it, but does not clearly state that a few visual examples communicate the concept more readily.

r002.rationale: It mentions describing how an object is moving, but does not state that temporal aspects make perceptual interactions harder to express in language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is a very powerful way of communicating, but it’s also a compressed representation of what we experience. There are a lot of things that are very easy to perceive and quite difficult to describe. If I show you two images of a room, you can immediately pick up on differences in the spatial arrangement, the lighting, or the texture of an object. Describing all of those differences in words can take a lot of effort, and you’ll probably still leave things out.

So if we want a system to understand the visual world, requiring it to express everything through language can introduce a bottleneck. It would be useful for it to represent those perceptual concepts directly, without having to first find the words for them.

r001.rationale: It says differences between two room images are immediately perceptible, while describing them in words takes effort and may leave things out.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a temporal component or how it makes perceptual interactions harder to express.
